newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Zaire cabinet holds emergency meeting.
newsitem.headline: Zaire cabinet holds emergency meeting.

text.p: Zaire's government held an emergency cabinet meeting on Monday in face of a relentless rebel advance on all fronts and against a backdrop of persistent rumours of an imminent coup.

With President Mobutu Sese Seko receiving fresh cancer treatment in hospital in Europe, officials said that the government was reviewing the way forward following the fall on Saturday of Zaire's third city of Kisangani.
"Perhaps they will decide to negotiate now. That would be the wisest thing," one source close to the government speculated.
Rebel leader Laurent Kabila has called for face-to-face talks with Mobutu, who had prostate cancer surgery in Europe in August and has been readmitted to hospital there for further treatment.
"You can't take a sick man out of his bed," the source close to the government added.

Kinshasa residents reported sporadic gunshots overnight around the teeming capital, where rumours of an imminent coup attempt are rife. In one incident, armed men opened fire from a car in the opposition stronghold of Limete.
Kisangani was headquarters for army operations in the war zone and an ill-fated January 20 government offensive.
It is strategically perched on the Zaire River which flows west to the capital 1,500 km (900 miles) downstream.

Rebels, who have been welcomed as liberators along their way, swept into central Kisangani almost unopposed on Saturday but said they met stiff resistance on the approaches during the preceeding days.

The government's notoriously ill-disciplined soldiers, who turned on their Serb mercenary allies at the international airport on the outskirts of town late on Friday, looted what they could and fled across the river.

The fall of the city sent a shudder through some members of the ruling class. "I don't know what to think," one senior government official said. "We don't know whether the troops will obey their commanders."
The Tutsi-led rebels took up arms in October, vowing to topple Mobutu, who seized power in 1965 and has dominated the sprawling Central Africa nation since then.
The rebels accused the Zairean authorities of denying them citizenship and planning to expel them to Rwanda, their ancestral home.
They and the opposition, which enjoys strong support in the capital, accuse Zaire's veteran leader of ruining Africa's potentially richest country.
